hints: Look at the boiling points in the table. Which oxides have very high boiling points above 1000 degrees and which one is very low at 45 degrees, and what does that tell you about giant versus simple structures?
Recall how bonding changes across Period 3 from left to right, from highly ionic metal oxides to covalent non-metal oxides, and decide where the changeover occurs.
walkthrough:
Sort by melting and boiling point clue**
You can read a lot from the boiling points. $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$, $\text{MgO}$, $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ and $\text{SiO}_2$ all boil near or above $1275^{\circ}\text{C}$. That very high value screams giant lattice that needs huge energy to break apart. $\text{SO}_3$ boils at only $45^{\circ}\text{C}$, so it must be small separate molecules held together weakly.

Assign ionic versus covalent across the period**
Think left to right. Sodium, magnesium and aluminium are metals with large electronegativity difference from oxygen, so their oxides are ionic. Silicon and sulfur are non-metals, so $\text{SiO}_2$ and $\text{SO}_3$ are covalent. This is the classic Period 3 change from ionic to covalent.

Assign giant versus simple**
Ionic oxides are all giant ionic lattices. $\text{SiO}_2$ is covalent but still giant because each Si bonds tetrahedrally to four O atoms in a continuous network. Only $\text{SO}_3$ is simple molecular with discrete $\text{SO}_3$ molecules. That explains its very low boiling point.

Final answer: bonding row: $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ ionic, $\text{MgO}$ ionic, $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ ionic, $\text{SiO}_2$ covalent, $\text{SO}_3$ covalent
structure row: $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ giant, $\text{MgO}$ giant, $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ giant, $\text{SiO}_2$ giant / macromolecular, $\text{SO}_3$ simple / molecular

hints: Recall from part (a) the structure of each oxide: which one is a giant network and which one exists as separate small molecules?
Identify what must be broken to boil each substance: strong covalent bonds throughout the lattice versus weak forces between molecules.
Link strength of attraction to energy needed, and therefore to boiling point.
walkthrough:
Picture what boiling means for each**
Do not think both are breaking the same thing. In $\text{SiO}_2$ every silicon is covalently bonded into a huge 3D network. To make it boil you must actually break strong $\text{Si-O}$ covalent bonds throughout that lattice. In $\text{SO}_3$ you have neat little $\text{SO}_3$ molecules. Boiling just pulls those molecules apart from each other.

Name the forces correctly**
For $\text{SiO}_2$, say strong covalent bonds, and stress many or network. For $\text{SO}_3$, the $\text{S=O}$ bonds inside each molecule stay intact on boiling. Only weak van der Waals forces or weak intermolecular forces between $\text{SO}_3$ molecules are overcome.

Compare the energy demand**
Strong covalent bonds need far more thermal energy to break than weak intermolecular forces need to overcome. That is why $\text{SiO}_2$ boils at $2950^{\circ}\text{C}$ while $\text{SO}_3$ boils at only $45^{\circ}\text{C}$.

Final answer: $\text{SiO}_2$ has a giant covalent network with many strong $\text{Si-O}$ covalent bonds to break.
$\text{SO}_3$ has a simple molecular structure with only weak van der Waals / intermolecular forces between molecules.
Much more energy is required to break the strong covalent bonds in $\text{SiO}_2$ than to overcome the weak intermolecular forces in $\text{SO}_3$, so $\text{SiO}_2$ has a much higher boiling point.

hints: Break the word amphoteric into its meaning: what two opposite types of reagent must the oxide react with?
Think of a familiar acid reaction of a metal oxide forming a salt plus water, and write it for $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ with $\text{HCl}$ or $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$.
Think of the alkali reaction forming a complex aluminate ion such as $\text{Al(OH)}_4^-$, and include $\text{NaOH}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ as reactants.
walkthrough:
Define amphoteric in one line**
Basic oxides react only with acids, acidic oxides react only with bases. Amphoteric sits in the middle and does both. So start your answer by stating it reacts with both an acid and a base or alkali.

Show the basic character with acid**
Acting as a base, $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ neutralises acid to give a normal aluminium salt plus water. A safe example is:
$$\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 6\text{HCl} \rightarrow 2\text{AlCl}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
Check balance: 2 Al, 6 H, 6 Cl and 3 O on each side.

Show the acidic character with alkali**
Acting as an acid, it reacts with sodium hydroxide to give sodium aluminate. The equation most examiners expect is:
$$\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 2\text{NaOH} + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{NaAl(OH)}_4$$
Here aluminium ends up in the $\text{Al(OH)}_4^-$ ion. Together the two equations prove amphoteric behaviour.

Final answer: Amphoteric means reacts with both acids and bases / alkalis.
With acid, e.g. $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 6\text{HCl} \rightarrow 2\text{AlCl}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$
With alkali, e.g. $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 2\text{NaOH} + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{NaAl(OH)}_4$

hints: Remember $\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ is a strongly basic soluble oxide, so think what happens to a solid alkali oxide when it meets water in terms of dissolving and heat.
walkthrough:
Visualise the vigorous basic reaction**
$\text{Na}_2\text{O}$ reacts readily: $\text{Na}_2\text{O} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{NaOH}$. From your viewpoint you would simply see the white solid vanish as it dissolves to form sodium hydroxide, and because the reaction is exothermic the solution feels warm or hot.
Final answer: Solid dissolves / disappears (to give colourless solution) OR mixture gets warm / hot (exothermic reaction).

hints: Count electron pairs around Se in $\text{SeF}_6$: how many bonding pairs and how many lone pairs, and which familiar $\text{SF}_6$ shape does this match?
walkthrough:
Apply VSEPR by analogy to sulfur**
Selenium is in Group 16 like sulfur, so $\text{SeF}_6$ is just like $\text{SF}_6$. Se forms six $\text{Se-F}$ bonding pairs and has no lone pairs left. Six bonding pairs with zero lone pairs repel to point to the six corners of an octahedron, with $90^{\circ}$ bond angles. So the shape is octahedral.
Final answer: Octahedral

hints: Use the description that one $\text{Se=O}$ is broken and two $\text{Se-O}$ are formed, and write $\Delta H$ = energy in for bonds broken minus energy out for bonds formed.
Substitute $\Delta H = -346 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ and $\text{Se=O} = 514 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$ and solve for the single $\text{Se-O}$ value.
walkthrough:
Translate the polymerisation into bonds**
Look at the diagram. Gaseous $\text{SeO}_2$ has two $\text{Se=O}$ double bonds. In the polymer unit one $\text{Se=O}$ remains and the other $\text{Se=O}$ has been replaced by two $\text{Se-O}$ single bonds linking to neighbours. So per mole: break 1 $\times$ $\text{Se=O}$, make 2 $\times$ $\text{Se-O}$.

Set up the bond enthalpy cycle**
Remember breaking is endothermic (+), making is exothermic (-). In one line:
$$\Delta H = \Sigma E(\text{broken}) - \Sigma E(\text{formed})$$
$$-346 = 514 - 2 \times E(\text{Se-O})$$
Rearrange: $2 \times E(\text{Se-O}) = 514 + 346 = 860$. So $E(\text{Se-O}) = 860 / 2 = 430 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$.

Final answer: $$\Delta H = E(\text{Se=O broken}) - 2E(\text{Se-O formed})$$
$$-346 = 514 - 2E(\text{Se-O})$$
bond enthalpy of $\text{Se-O} = 430 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$

hints: Recall the reaction of the analogous acidic oxide $\text{SO}_2$ with $\text{NaOH}$ to give sodium sulfite plus water, then replace S by Se.
walkthrough:
Copy the sulfur chemistry**
You are told $\text{SeO}_2$ reacts like $\text{SO}_2$. $\text{SO}_2$ is acidic and neutralised by alkali:
$$\text{SO}_2 + 2\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
Just swap S for Se to give sodium selenite:
$$\text{SeO}_2 + 2\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{SeO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$
